html:
The Finnish famine of 1866 to 1868 killed about 150,000 people, close to a tenth of the population of Finland. It was the last great peacetime famine in western Europe.

A wet summer in 1866 ruined the harvest, and in 1867 a very late spring and early frost destroyed the next. People ate bread made with pine bark. Beggars took to the roads, carrying typhus and other diseases, which killed most of the victims.

The government of the Grand Duchy was slow to borrow money for grain, fearing for the new currency. The famine pushed reforms in farming and poor relief, and it hit neighbouring Sweden too, adding to emigration. Compare the Irish Famine. See Finland.
